meta.title: Who really said "There's a hell of a distance between wise-cracking and wit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dorothy Parker really said it — to Marion Capron for The Paris Review, Issue 13, Summer 1956. Verified wording, source and US rights status.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There's a hell of a distance between wise-cracking and wit'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Parker's line comes from her 1956 Paris Review interview with Marion Capron. Full citation, wording variants and rights status.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and pinnable to a specific interview: Parker said it to Marion Capron in “The Art of Fiction, No. 13,” published in The Paris Review, Issue 13 (Summer 1956) and later collected in Writers at Work ↗. It was said in English, so no translation stands between you and the wording — only a hyphen, which several printings drop (“wisecracking”).

source.heading: The source, in full

docMeta.dd: Writers at Work: The Paris Review Interviews, First Series (1958)

source.excerpt:
INTERVIEWER. You have an extensive reputation as a wit. Has this interfered, do you think, with your acceptance as a serious writer?

PARKER. I don’t want to be classed as a humorist. It makes me feel guilty. … A “smartcracker” they called me, and that makes me sick and unhappy. There’s a hell of a distance between wise-cracking and wit. Wit has truth in it; wise-cracking is simply calisthenics with words.
trail: Specialist check. Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page ↗ carries the full two-sentence quotation in its sourced Quotes section, cited to “Interview, The Paris Review (Summer 1956)” — not under Misattributed and not under Disputed.

The bibliographic citation. WIST Quotations ↗ gives the source as Interview (1956, Summer), “The Art of Fiction, No. 13,” by Marion Capron, The Paris Review, Issue 13, and records that it was collected in Writers at Work: The Paris Review Interviews, First Series (1958).

The line in situ. An online reproduction of the interview ↗ shows the sentence as Parker’s answer to a question about her reputation as a wit, immediately after she rejects the labels “humorist” and “smartcracker.” It prints the word unhyphenated.

The company it keeps. Quote Investigator ↗ documents Parker as a standing magnet for quips she never made — which is exactly why a Parker line that can be pinned to an issue and an interviewer is worth pinning.
source.excerptNote: The two-sentence quotation is confirmed independently by Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ and WIST ↗. The surrounding question and the “smartcracker” sentence come from an online reproduction of the interview ↗, which prints “wisecracking” without the hyphen; the ellipsis marks two sentences cut from the middle of Parker’s answer.

source.rightsNote: The words come from an interview first published in The Paris Review, Issue 13, in the summer of 1956 — well after the 1931 threshold that governs public-domain status in the United States — so the text is in copyright, not public domain. Rights sit with The Paris Review as first publisher and with Parker’s literary estate, which she bequeathed to Martin Luther King Jr. and, upon King’s death, to the NAACP ↗. Quoting the sentence with attribution, as here, is ordinary citation; reproducing the interview at length is not.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: Who Dorothy Parker was
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic & screenwriter; founding member of the Algonquin Round Table
author.bio: Dorothy Parker (born 22 August 1893, died 7 June 1967) was an American poet, short-story writer, critic and screenwriter, and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table — the New York lunch circle whose reputation for repartee she spent much of her later life trying to shrug off. Her verse and stories are compressed, unsentimental and often savage, and she twice earned Academy Award nominations for screenwriting. She left her estate to Martin Luther King Jr. and, on his death, to the NAACP — a bequest that still surprises readers who know her only as a dispenser of one-liners.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nothing here is misattributed — the line really is Parker’s, and it sits in a sourced section rather than a disputed one. What travels badly is the wording, the truncation, and the company the quotation keeps.

items.why: Both spellings circulate, citing the same 1956 interview. Wikiquote ↗ and Interesting Literature ↗ print the hyphenated form; WIST ↗ and an online reproduction of the interview ↗ print it closed up. The sense is identical; we render the hyphenated form because that is how the line most often circulates.

The half most people meet ends at “… and wit,” dropping the sentence that supplies the criterion. WIST records the quotation as the second sentence ↗ — “Wit has truth in it; wisecracking is simply calisthenics with words” — which is where the argument actually lives.

Parker is one of the most over-credited names in English. Quote Investigator ↗ documents commentators of the 1930s and 1940s complaining that every New York wisecrack got hung on her, and Parker herself conceding in 1941 that she had not originated most of them. Even the celebrated protest line — “Everything I’ve ever said will be credited to Dorothy Parker,” ascribed to George S. Kaufman — is shaky: QI traces it to Scott Meredith’s 1974 biography, more than a decade after Kaufman’s death in 1961, with no earlier primary documentation.

misattribution.truthLine: This one survives the scrutiny. The line was given to Marion Capron and published in The Paris Review, Issue 13, Summer 1956, and Wikiquote carries it in its sourced section ↗ — and it is, pointedly, Parker objecting to being called a wisecracker.

context.heading: It is a complaint, not a boast
lead: The line is almost always quoted as Dorothy Parker being clever about cleverness. In the interview it is the opposite: a writer pushing back. Marion Capron had just asked whether her extensive reputation as a wit had got in the way of her being accepted as a serious writer, and Parker’s answer opens by refusing the category outright — she does not want to be classed as a humorist, and the label “smartcracker” makes her, in her words, sick and unhappy.

The distinction she then draws is doing real work. Wisecracking is a performance skill — timing, symmetry, a word turned over at speed. Wit, on her account, has to be about something true. That is a standard she is applying to herself, and it is a harsher one than her public reputation ever asked of her.
context.detailsSummary: Why the one-sentence version loses the argument
detailsBody: The quotation circulates almost everywhere as a single sentence: There’s a hell of a distance between wise-cracking and wit. On its own that is a claim without a criterion — it asserts a gap and never says what fills it.

The second sentence is the whole argument. WIST files the quotation under that second sentence ↗ rather than the first, which is a fair editorial judgement: “wit has truth in it” is the test, and “calisthenics with words” is the verdict on what fails it.
context.pull: Wit has truth in it; wise-cracking is simply calisthenics with words.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Dorothy Parker page carries "There's a hell of a distance between wise-cracking and wit. Wit has truth in it; wise-cracking is simply calisthenics with words." in its main sourced Quotes section, cited to Interview, The Paris Review (Summer 1956) — not under Misattributed or Disputed.

WIST Quotations gives "Wit has truth in it; wisecracking is simply calisthenics with words." sourced to Interview (1956, Summer), "The Art of Fiction, No. 13," by Marion Capron, The Paris Review, Issue 13, and notes it was collected in Writers at Work: The Paris Review Interviews, First Series (1958). It prints "wisecracking" unhyphenated.
WIST's index page for the same interview confirms the citation form "Interview (1956, Summer), 'The Art of Fiction, No. 13,' by Marion Capron, The Paris Review, Issue 13".

This page reproduces the Paris Review "Art of Fiction" interview and shows the interviewer asking whether Parker's reputation as a wit interfered with her acceptance as a serious writer, with Parker answering that she does not want to be classed as a humorist, that "A 'smartcracker' they called me, and that makes me sick and unhappy", and then "There's a hell of a distance between wisecracking and wit. Wit has truth in it; wisecracking is simply calisthenics with words."

Quote Investigator documents that Dorothy Parker was a magnet for misquotations, that 1930s–1940s commentary complained every New York wisecrack was attributed to her, that Parker acknowledged in 1941 she did not originate most quips credited to her, and that "Everything I've ever said will be credited to Dorothy Parker" is ascribed to George S. Kaufman only via Scott Meredith's 1974 biography — more than a decade after Kaufman's death in 1961, with no earlier primary documentation.

Interesting Literature lists "There's a hell of a distance between wise-cracking and wit. Wit has truth in it; wise-cracking is simply calisthenics with words." cited to "Interview in Paris Review, 1956", in a list the page says is confined to things Parker definitely did say.

Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker's dates as born 22 August 1893 and died 7 June 1967, describes her as a poet, literary critic, screenwriter and founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, and states: "In her will, she bequeathed her estate to Martin Luther King Jr., and upon King's death, to the NAACP."

The Internet Archive catalogues a scanned copy of "Writers At Work: the Paris Review Interviews" with creator Malcolm Cowley and publisher Viking, dated 1959 (confirmed via the archive.org metadata endpoint for this item).

The Paris Review's own page for "Dorothy Parker, The Art of Fiction No. 13" is the canonical home of the interview.
